blocks.text: (Conclusion). As long as the doves cannot yet fly, they move at most 50 cubits away from the dovecote, or in general [p. 202] only so far as not to lose sight of the dovecote (Beza 11a). With regard to age, various points in time were designated according to which certain ritual rulings were made. As long as the dove is still so young that no blood flows when the feathers are plucked, it is unfit for sacrifice and does not yet belong to the category of בני יונה which the Law (Lev. 1, 14) designates for sacrifice. On the other hand, it bears the latter name as long as it has not yet acquired the metallic-coloured (צהב) feathers around the neck; but as soon as these feathers appear it ceases to be called בני יונה, yet receives the name תור (which denotes not so much the turtle-dove in particular as the full-grown dove in general) only once the remaining feathers have become yellow-coloured (זהב) (Chulin 22b). This designated interval thus forms a provisional state in which the dove is called neither בני יונה nor תור. In young doves, skin and flesh are equally soft (ibid. 76b).

It was believed that the dove has no gall (Jore Dea §. 42, 8), which Isidorus (Orig. lib. 12) and Sedulius (L. 2, Carm.) also report; it does, however, have a gall, which is located in the mesentery (Plin. h. n. 11, 37, 75).

When drinking, the dove sucks up the water without raising its head (Chulin 62b), and the water does not flow back out of the beak (Para 9, 3), whereas the latter is the case with the tumbler pigeon (§. 254).
The common house pigeon and the tumbler pigeon sometimes hatch each other's eggs (Chulin 140b).

A particularly destructive enemy of doves is the marten, which is why the ladder was kept four cubits away from the dovecote, so that the predator could not jump into it (B. batra 22b). The fertility of doves is great, for except in the month of Adar (a late winter month) they breed every month and bring forth a pair, male and female. After two months the young doves already lay eggs and brood (B. batra 80a). King Janai had a mountain on which stood a tree from which 40 measures of young doves (קוביש, couvées) were taken down three times a month (Berachoth 44a); but here it is more probably the wild dove (§. 255) that is meant.
The flesh of young doves is tasty, and a notorious glutton named Ben Narboni consumed for dessert (!)
[p. 203] the trifle of 4 measures of young doves (Keritot 28a.*).

For all this, the dove also causes much damage. One was not permitted to keep dovecotes within the town, since the doves did damage to the surrounding gardens, and it was permitted only to one whose house had 50 cubits of open space on all sides (B. batra 23a). They eat in particular the grain laid out on the roofs to dry (Tos. ibid. s.v. מרחיקין).

The dove does fly away from the house, but it is harmful only within the space of the first 50 cubits, since by then its crop is full and it eats nothing more (ibid.). A particular favourite food of the dove is mustard (Sabbat 128a).

Wagers were made as to whose dove would fly first, or how long it would fly (R. ha-Schana 22a). It was wrongful to lure doves away, and one who did this was called ארא (Rashi אשחלין, stellionate, Sanhedrin 25a). Nor was one permitted to set up snares within 30 Riß (= 4 Mil or 8000 cubits) of the town (B. Kama 79b).

Of the turtle-dove, this dainty and graceful bird, there are many varieties and sub-varieties, some of which are mentioned in the Talmud. The general name for all kinds is תור, pl. תורין (Chulin 22a), and there are large and small turtle-doves, i.e. different varieties of it (ibid.); but even the actual turtle-dove bears the name תור only once the feathers acquire the yellow colour, i.e. when the back, the rump and the upper tail feathers become brown-spotted and isabelline yellow (ibid. 22b).
On the name קן see §. 252, at the end.

A variety of the turtle-dove, which however can hardly be determined precisely, is the one under the name ראציפי (Chulin 62a), for which Aruch reads דריציפי, and with which he identifies ציצלא (Sanhedrin 100a, [p. 204] where, however, צילצלא is written). In the first passage it is said that the דאציפי may be taken as a sacrifice in place of the תורים, but not in place of the בני יונה; accordingly they must stand in size between the full-grown turtle-dove and the young, still small dove.

In Sanhedrin ibid. and Sabbat 80b the egg of the צינילתא (fem. of צילצלא) is used to designate a small object. In both passages Rashi explains the bird's name vaguely as עוף קטן (small bird), which, however, could very well mean the variety of turtle-dove. The largest species of turtle-dove is scarcely a foot long; accordingly צינילתא must, by the proportion of size mentioned above, be smaller still, and in the same proportion the egg will then also be smaller, indeed such that it could serve to designate a small object.
On B. batra 75a Samuel explains צילצלא as חאציל, which is perhaps the same as חסיל (§. 254).
Metonymically the turtle-dove is also called קן (Nedarim 35b).
